aliases: Шу пуэр мини то ча с лотосом
processing: Ripe pu-erh combined with lotus material for aroma and commonly pressed into small tuos. Exactly which part of the lotus is used, and how, differs by producer.
harvest_season: No defined season; it is made from ordinary ripe pu-erh base tea, and the pressing year matters more than the picking.
appearance_dry: Small, dark brown pressed tuos, each roughly a single pot's portion.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft dark brown leaf fragments with any lotus material mixed in.
taste_profile: Typically an earthy, smooth ripe base with a green, sweetly aquatic lotus aroma; intensity varies a lot between makers.

brewing.notes: One mini tuo usually makes one small pot. Rinse once to loosen it, then steep; the tight centre needs a round or two to open.

vintage_note: Usually sold as a convenient everyday tea, loose by weight or in tins, with little focus on vintage. Aroma from an added flower fades over time, so drink it within a few years instead of cellaring it.
description:
He xiang means lotus fragrance. In the shops this is mostly a mini tuo: a small ball of ripe pu-erh with lotus aroma, sized so one piece fills one small pot.

The base is ordinary wet-piled shu. The lotus element varies, and the packaging does not always say whether it comes from leaf, flower or added flavouring, so the same name can cover quite different teas.

In the cup it should still read as ripe pu-erh, dark and smooth, with a cool green-sweet perfume over it. Near-boiling water suits it. Too long a steep buries the lotus under the pile note.

When buying, check the ingredients for flavouring and smell the dry tuo: a soft plant aroma is a better sign than a loud perfume. Do not expect individual tuos to be high grade, since the format is built for convenience.
history: Little is documented about the origin of lotus-scented ripe pu-erh. It appears today mainly as a commercial mini tuo from various makers, and no originator or starting date is established.
